rows.subtype: Approach: making a feeding and cleaning schedule [Action]
rows.description: A boy with a new puppy writes feeding at seven and six, walk after school and water bowl check, and pins it near the door so the family follows it consistently.

rows.subtype: Approach: observing the animal's behaviour to understand needs [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl notices her cat hides and stops eating, and thinks something may be wrong instead of assuming it is only sulking, then asks her mother to call the vet.

rows.subtype: Approach: enthusiasm early and neglect later [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child begs for a rabbit and cares for it eagerly for two weeks, but as the novelty fades, the parents end up feeding it, showing that caring is a daily commitment.

rows.subtype: Approach: learning from a mistake with the pet [Revision]
rows.description: After leaving the fish tank in direct sun and finding the water too warm, the girl moves it to a shaded corner and adds a thermometer reading to her daily checks.

rows.subtype: Approach: watching the queue [Thinking]
rows.description: A child at the slide counts the children ahead and works out, "Three more, then me." Knowing the place in the line makes the waiting easier to bear.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking an adult [Action]
rows.description: Another child skips ahead on the swing, so a child says to the teacher, "He didn't wait his turn." The adult is used to settle whose turn it is.

rows.subtype: Approach: pushing in [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child squeezes to the front of the line for the slide, and the others shout. The turn is got for a moment and the friendship pays for it.

rows.subtype: Approach: trial and error [Revision]
rows.description: Shouting "my turn" got a child nowhere. Next day the child asks, "Can I go after you?" and the child on the swing agrees. Polite asking is kept as the new plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: laying out all income, debts and goals openly [Thinking]
rows.description: Newly married, a couple lists salaries, education loan EMIs, savings and plans. Seeing the whole picture together lets them reason as one team rather than guess about each other.

rows.subtype: Approach: values-first planning about saving versus spending [Thinking]
rows.description: One partner wants to save for a flat, the other values travel. They agree on a percentage for each goal, so neither feels their priority is dismissed.

rows.subtype: Approach: one partner managing everything without discussion [Pitfall]
rows.description: Assuming it is easier, the husband handles all money matters. His wife does not know the loans or savings, and a sudden expense causes tension and mistrust.

rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the rules when circumstances change [Revision]
rows.description: After one partner changes jobs and the income drops, they hold a special meeting, cut two categories and adjust contributions. Rules are treated as a working agreement rather than a fixed law.

rows.subtype: Approach: clarifying the goal and the one key message [Thinking]
rows.description: Before telling her father she is leaving the family business, she decides her aim is to be understood, not to win. She reduces her points to one clear sentence.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of possible reactions [Thinking]
rows.description: She imagines her mother crying, her father staying silent, or an argument starting. For each reaction she prepares a calm reply and a way to pause the talk if needed.

rows.subtype: Approach: putting it off until the last moment [Pitfall]
rows.description: She delays telling her parents about her plan to move abroad, and they hear it from a relative. The news lands worse, and trust is hurt more than the decision itself.

rows.subtype: Approach: sleeping on it and planning a follow-up talk [Revision]
rows.description: When the first talk becomes heated, he says let us continue tomorrow. The next day, both are calmer and reach a plan, showing that a difficult conversation can be split across several days.

rows.subtype: Approach: checking the rule that adults ask adults [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy is asked by a man to help find a lost puppy in his car, and thinks that grown-ups normally ask other grown-ups for help, so this request is odd and needs caution.

rows.subtype: Approach: saying no and walking to a trusted adult [Action]
rows.description: The girl refuses to go anywhere with the person, keeps a distance, moves toward the guard at the gate and tells him what was asked, then informs her parents at home.

rows.subtype: Approach: going along because refusing feels rude [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child who has been taught to always be polite to elders follows a stranger who says her mother is hurt, and only later realises that politeness should not override safety.

rows.subtype: Approach: telling a parent even when unsure [Revision]
rows.description: After a stranger asked her to come along and she froze, a girl feels ashamed and hides it at first, then decides telling her mother is safer, and the family adds a plan to it.

rows.subtype: Approach: emotion-aware planning of the first weeks [Thinking]
rows.description: The student accepts that the first weeks will be heavy and plans around it, keeping routines like classes, meals and sleep, and not making big decisions on bad days.

rows.subtype: Approach: leaning on friends and family [Action]
rows.description: The student tells two close friends what happened, accepts invitations even when not in the mood, and calls a sibling weekly, so that isolation does not deepen the pain.

rows.subtype: Approach: checking the ex's profiles repeatedly [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student keeps looking at the ex's posts hoping for a sign, and each look reopens the hurt, while the habit keeps the breakup fresh long after it ended.

rows.subtype: Approach: seeking professional support when low persists [Revision]
rows.description: When sadness stays heavy for two months and affects studies, the student books a campus counsellor visit instead of waiting, and starts to feel more supported.
